name: Uma Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Uma, thanks for doing this. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and everything you say is confidential. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach the reception class at St Bride's, a private prep school, so it's eighteen four- and five-year-olds. I'm in at quarter to eight setting up the water tray, the sand and the phonics cards, and then it's a blur of shoelaces, snack, story time and someone crying about a lost sticker. I love when a child reads their first word off a card and looks at me like they've done magic. What wears me out is the written observations, because I have to log every child's progress on the tablet and I'm still slow at it.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with Tom, my partner, who's an electrician. Private schools pay a bit more than state ones here, and we've saved well, about nine months of costs, plus premium bonds my grandparents bought me. I'm not political, I just vote for whoever seems sensible. I use AI sometimes, like when the other teachers showed me it can write the newsletter, but I'm not first in the queue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's that then. Most of the parents at St Bride's work in offices and talk about AI all the time at pick-up, so I'd just nod along. I wouldn't post anything; I don't really post about work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, nothing much changes for me. You can't use AI to change a nappy accident or calm a crying four-year-old. If it writes the newsletter and helps with the observations, lovely, that's an hour back on a Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am and use AI for the newsletter, which I already do sometimes. I'd ask the head of early years to sit with me on the observation app, because I'm behind on my logs. We'd keep saving and maybe book a holiday to Japan to see my grandmother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Nothing to lose sleep over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything already worrying you about work, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My observation logs are behind, and the inspection's due next year. My head of early years is kind about it, but I know she's noticed. That's the main thing on my mind, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the Friday hour?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Make better resources, probably. I'd love to build a proper role-play corner, like a little vet's surgery, with real bandages and a toy stethoscope. Kids learn more from a role-play corner with real bandages and a toy stethoscope than from any screen.

say: I'd say **that's that** and nod along with parents talking AI at pick-up.
I'd **not post** anything, since I keep work offline.
think: You can't use AI to calm a **crying four-year-old**, so little changes for me.
If it helps with **observations**, I'd gain an hour back on Fridays.
do: Keep using AI for the **class newsletter**.
Ask the head of early years for help with the **observation app**.
Keep saving and book a trip to **see my grandmother**.
feel: **Calm**, with nothing to lose sleep over.
S0.quote: Kids learn more from a role-play corner with real bandages and a toy stethoscope than from any screen.
fieldNote: Her day is mostly **hands-on care**, which AI barely touches.
Her real pressure is **behind-schedule logs** before an inspection.
She's **steady**: uses AI where colleagues showed her it works.

steps.text: Use AI to draft the weekly class newsletter
Book a session on the observation app with the head of early years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to change a lot of jobs and people need help adjusting. At pick-up I'd say little ones still need people, and the parents would agree. I'd keep it friendly and practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job is pretty safe, because early years is all hands-on. The worry is the parents. Most of them are lawyers, bankers, consultants, and if their jobs shrink, some of them stop paying fees, and the school takes fewer children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the observation app and any AI that helps with the logs once the other teachers are using it. I'd keep an eye on the school roll; if it drops, I'd look at state school jobs nearby, and there are plenty. I'd keep saving and maybe hold off on the Japan trip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for my job exactly, but for the school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know if the school was in trouble?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Empty pegs. If I've only got fourteen names on pegs instead of eighteen in September, that's the sign the school is in trouble. The bursar would start talking about merging classes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Tom say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tom would say electricians will be fine for ages, and that he could carry us if needed. He's right, really. He's never short of work.

say: I'd say lots of jobs will change and **people need help** adjusting.
At pick-up I'd say **little ones** still need people.
think: Early years is **hands-on**, so my own job looks safe.
If office **parents' jobs** shrink, fewer pay fees and the school shrinks.
do: Learn the AI **observation tools** once other teachers use them.
Watch the **school roll** and look at state schools if it drops.
**Hold off** on the Japan trip and keep saving.
feel: **Uneasy**, more for the school than for my own job.
S1.quote: If I've only got fourteen names on pegs instead of eighteen in September, that's the sign the school is in trouble.
fieldNote: She spots a **second-order risk**: fee-paying parents in exposed office jobs.
Her **partner's trade** makes the household feel secure.
Plenty of **state school jobs** nearby is her backup.

steps.text: Learn the AI observation logging tool after colleagues adopt it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need the government to look after people quickly, because this would hit a lot of families at once. I'd say small children still need a real adult. I'd stay calm in front of the parents, because they'd be panicking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the school could be in real trouble by 2029. If AGI does the parents' jobs, they can't pay fees, and private schools close. The children still need someone hands-on till robots come in 2031, and maybe after, but I'd need to be in a state school, not a private one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move to a state primary within a year, before the private sector shakes out and everyone's applying at once. I'd keep our savings in cash and not touch the premium bonds. I'd learn whatever AI tools the new school uses, once I saw them work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. My skills still matter, but the private school that pays me might not survive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a state school pay you less?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit less, yes, maybe a few thousand a year. But it's steadier, especially if governments put money into schools. I'd rather a smaller wage that lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Tom's work with robots coming in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tom would have the three extra years, and then wiring old houses is fiddly; I can't see a robot doing it soon. I'd be leaning on him for a while, but he'd lean on me later. That's how we work.

say: I'd ask the government to **help families** quickly.
I'd say small children still need **a real adult**, and stay calm for parents.
think: If AGI takes parents' jobs, **fees stop** and private schools close.
Children still need hands-on care **till 2031**, but in **state schools**.
do: Move to a **state primary** within a year, before the rush.
Keep savings in **cash** and leave the premium bonds alone.
Learn the new school's **AI tools** once proven.
feel: **Anxious**, because the place that pays me might not survive.
S2.quote: My skills still matter, but the private school that pays me might not survive.
fieldNote: Her **employer's survival** is the risk, not her own skills.
She plans to **move early**, before everyone else applies.
She sees her partnership as **taking turns** leaning on each other.

steps.text: Apply to state primary schools within the year
Keep savings in cash and leave the premium bonds
Learn the new school's AI tools after seeing them work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives schools and families time to get ready. I'd say early years teachers will still be needed. I'd keep it simple and hopeful at pick-up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I've got time to see how St Bride's does. If fees start dropping in 2029 or 2030, I'd move before 2031. My hands-on work keeps me going past that, at least till the robots around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at St Bride's for now and keep my eyes open. I'd take a short course in special needs in the early years, because that's always wanted in state schools. We'd go to Japan this year after all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit watchful. Not scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you look out for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bursar's emails, class sizes, whether they freeze pay. If the school freezes pay two years running, I'd start applying elsewhere. That's my line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would it change anything with Tom, like plans for a family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We want kids in about four years. Five years' warning wouldn't change that. If anything, I'd want to be in a state school by then for the maternity pay.

say: I'd say **five years** gives schools and families time to prepare.
I'd say early years teachers will **still be needed**.
think: I'd watch St Bride's and **move before 2031** if fees fall.
Hands-on work keeps me going **till about 2034**.
do: Stay at the school and **watch for warning signs**.
Take a short course in **early years special needs**.
Go ahead with the **Japan trip** this year.
S3.quote: If the school freezes pay two years running, I'd start applying elsewhere.
fieldNote: She sets a **clear trigger**: two years of pay freeze.
**Special needs** training is her portable skill for state schools.
Family plans tie to **maternity pay** in state schools.

steps.text: Stay at St Bride's and watch for two years of pay freezes
Take a short early years special needs course
Plan a move to a state school before having children

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and people will adapt. I'd say children will always need caring adults. I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be absolutely fine. By 2036 I'd be thirty-seven, experienced, maybe with my own kids, and early years is hands-on till 2039 at the earliest. Even then, I don't think parents will hand a four-year-old to a robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at St Bride's and get really good at early years. I'd pick up the AI tools for paperwork when the school does. We'd keep saving for a bigger house and kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, just a little. Ten years is far off, and a decade of AI doesn't really touch the sandpit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything you'd worry about over ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The teaching assistants, maybe, and the office. Our school secretary books everything and answers every parent email, and that's exactly what AI does first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the government to do with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep funding early years properly and train more people for it. Every child should have a caring adult at four, not a tablet.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a long time, and people and schools will adapt.
I'd say children always need **caring adults**.
think: By **2036** I'd be experienced, and early years stays hands-on till 2039.
I doubt parents would hand a **four-year-old** to a robot.
do: Stay at the school and **master early years** teaching.
Adopt AI **paperwork tools** when the school does.
Keep saving for a **bigger house** and children.
feel: **Uneasy** only a little, because it's far off.
S4.quote: Ten years is far off, and a decade of AI doesn't really touch the sandpit.
fieldNote: Her work is the **least exposed** of most teaching, and she knows it.
Her worry shifts to **office and support staff**.
She wants **early years funding** protected over the decade.

steps.text: Keep teaching reception at St Bride's
Use the school's AI paperwork tools once adopted
Save monthly towards a bigger house with Tom

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because private schools would fold so fast. What would help is the government funding more state early years places, so teachers like me have somewhere to go.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that people forget the youngest children. Every four-year-old needs a person who knows their name and their snack order. No machine is going to love them back.

headlineQuote: Every four-year-old needs a person who knows their name and their snack order.
